edges.effect_quant: In a 164-patient Roux-en-Y cohort, iron deficiency developed in 42.3% of women and 22.0% of men, and a long-term adolescent bariatric meta-analysis of 4970 patients found postoperative iron deficiency in 23% and low ferritin in 49%.
edges.population: patients after Roux-en-Y gastric bypass and related bariatric bypass procedures
edges.mechanism: Bypass of the stomach and proximal small bowel impairs the acid-mediated solubilization and duodenal absorption that ordinarily support iron uptake, while lower intake and intolerance of iron-rich foods can further worsen repletion. Menstruation and low baseline ferritin magnify the effect.
edges.summary: Iron deficiency is one of the most common nutritional complications after gastric bypass, and the risk often persists or worsens with longer follow-up. Oral replacement alone may be insufficient in a meaningful fraction of patients, which is why ferritin surveillance and aggressive supplementation protocols are standard post-bypass care.
edges.caveats: Procedure type, sex, baseline iron stores, and supplement adherence strongly influence prevalence estimates. Although the risk is high, it is also manageable when monitoring is structured and intravenous or higher-dose repletion is used when oral iron fails.
